title: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering
guide: Functions work only across a narrow pH range; daily H⁺ production is 7 crore nmol against a blood H⁺ of 40 nmol/L at pH 7.4. Excess H⁺ is cellulotoxic, altering cellular morphology before the buffering system renders it safe. Buffering types: chemical (immediate), respiratory (fast), renal (slow). Chemical buffering = [H⁺] + [A⁻] → HA, with H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ the most potent extracellular buffer; pKa is the pH at which 50% A⁻ = 50% HA, and weak acids (mostly A⁻) are the best buffers.

title: The Siggaard–Andersen nomogram and the three buffer types
guide: Nomogram: x-axis arterial pH 7.0–7.8, y-axis arterial plasma HCO₃⁻ 0–60 mmol/L, right-hand [H⁺] scale 100→20 nmol/L, isobars labelled pCO₂ 120→10 mmHg, and printed zones for normal, acute/chronic respiratory acidosis and alkalosis, and metabolic acidosis/alkalosis. Buffer types: bicarbonate system (1st compensation in metabolic acidosis, CO₂ exhaled so PaCO₂ falls = 2nd compensation), phosphate (pKa 6.8, 2nd most effective, better intracellularly) and haemoglobin (pKa 7.3, best intracellular buffer).

title: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA
guide: Causes of metabolic acidosis = acid generation (exogenous: methanol; endogenous: ketoacids) and alkali loss (GI and renal). Anion gap derivation from measured/unmeasured cations and anions, giving AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). NAGMA = hyperchloremic acidosis with GI loss (VIPoma, ureterosigmoidostomy) and renal loss (RTA); HAGMA = rise in unmeasured anions with the KUSMAL list — ketoacidosis (DKA, starvation, alcoholic), uremia, salicylates/paraldehyde, methanol, ethylene glycol (alcohol) and lactic acidosis.

title: Terminology, H⁺ estimation and the buffering systems
guide: Acidemia < 7.36, alkalemia > 7.44, with acidosis/alkalosis defined as those states left unopposed. H⁺ estimation: 40 nmol/L at pH 7.4, ×1.25 per 0.1 pH fall, ×0.8 per 0.1 pH rise (7.2 = 63, 7.3 = 50, 7.5 = 32, 7.6 = 25). Respiratory buffering drives CO₂ out with ↑ respiratory rate → respiratory alkalosis → ↓PaCO₂. Renal buffering: non-volatile acids (sulphuric, phosphoric) excreted 1 mEq/kg/day (80 mEq/day) as titratable acid and ammonia; volatile H₂CO₃ is exhaled. 4330 mEq/day of HCO₃⁻ (24 × 180 L) is filtered and 100% reabsorbed — PCT ≈ 4000 mEq > thick AL > DCT — so urine HCO₃⁻ is nil.

title: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram
guide: Luminal Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger; luminal CA IV converts HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ to H₂CO₃ (step ①), which splits into H₂O + CO₂ (step ②). CO₂ enters the cell where CA II rebuilds H₂CO₃ (step ③), which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ (step ④); HCO₃⁻ leaves on the basolateral Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger. H₂O, Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ are reabsorbed along with CO₂.

title: Proximal (type 2) RTA: the 4400 mEq H⁺ problem and the PCT defect
guide: For 1 mEq HCO₃⁻ reabsorbed, 1 mEq H⁺ is used; 4330 mEq of HCO₃⁻ plus 80 mEq of non-volatile acid demands 4400 mEq H⁺ daily — not practically possible, hence the requirement of the buffering system. Type 2 RTA = generalised PCT dysfunction from a Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger or carbonic anhydrase defect: Fanconi's syndrome in childhood (cystinosis m/c, Lowe's disease, Wilson disease in adolescence) and myeloma or drugs (tenofovir, cyclophosphamide, outdated tetracycline, gentamicin) in adults. The PCT defect cascades to NAGMA, salt water wasting, RAS activation and hypokalemia; the phosphate arm gives rickets-like changes and the glucose arm glycosuria.

title: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion
guide: Cortical collecting system diagram of the α-intercalated cell: luminal H⁺-ATPase and H⁺,K⁺-ATPase (both ATP-dependent), cytoplasmic CA II making H₂CO₃ from CO₂ and H₂O, and H⁺ secreted into the lumen. HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻ is titratable acid and NH₃ → NH₄⁺ is non-titratable acid. Net acid secretion = urine NH₄⁺ + urine titratable acid − urine HCO₃⁻.

title: Distal (type 1) RTA and the distal vs proximal RTA table
guide: Distal RTA = H⁺-ATPase / H⁺,K⁺-ATPase defect, giving severe NAGMA, severe hypokalemia, salt water wasting with RANS activation, ↑Ca²⁺ resorption in bone with rickets-like change and kidney stones, an alkaline urine and no glycosuria. The distal vs proximal table: severity of NAGMA + hypokalemia (severe vs mild), mechanism of rickets (Ca²⁺ resorption vs loss of phosphorus), stones (present vs absent), urine pH (alkaline vs normal), glycosuria (absent vs present), inherited causes (AR H⁺ ATPase/H⁺ K⁺ ATPase defect vs Fanconi's syndrome) and acquired causes (Sjögren's syndrome vs myeloma).

title: Urine anion gap and the ammonia-forming pathway
guide: Urine anion gap = urinary Na⁺ + urinary K⁺ − urinary Cl⁻ = unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation, normally slightly negative. A positive UAG indicates RTA; a negative UAG indicates GI loss. Ammonia formation is predominantly in the proximal tubules from glutamine → glutamate → α-keto glutarate, releasing NH₃ at each step.
